reason: The sources provide over a dozen cross-verified claims across multiple distinct websites detailing IC 1101's history, extreme scale, and ongoing growth.
story: On June 19, 1790, astronomer William Herschel discovered a faint celestial smudge in the constellation Virgo. Today, we know that smudge as IC 1101, a supergiant galaxy anchored at the center of the Abell 2029 galaxy cluster over one billion light-years away from Earth. Recent ultra-deep observations using the Isaac Newton Telescope revealed that IC 1101 spans an astonishing 1.7 million light-years in diameter. If it were positioned between our Milky Way and the Andromeda Galaxy, its main stellar body would stretch almost the entire gap between them. Containing trillions of solar masses in stars, this cosmic colossus grew into a monster by cannibalizing neighboring galaxies over billions of years. Even more mind-bending, astronomers found that IC 1101 has not stopped feeding: faint plume-like remnants in its outskirts show that this cosmic giant is actively devouring nearby galactic debris and continuing to grow.
angle: If the supergiant galaxy IC 1101 were placed between the Milky Way and the Andromeda Galaxy, its stellar body would span almost the entire distance between them.

claims.claim: IC 1101 was discovered on June 19, 1790, by astronomer William Herschel.
IC 1101 is located at the center of the Abell 2029 galaxy cluster.
IC 1101 is located approximately one billion light-years away from Earth.
IC 1101 has a measured main body diameter of about 1.7 million light-years (520 kiloparsecs).
IC 1101 is considered the largest or one of the largest known galaxies in the universe.
The ultra-deep imaging of IC 1101 was conducted using the Isaac Newton Telescope at the Roque de los Muchachos Observatory.
The deep imaging study of IC 1101 was led by Carlos Marrero-de la Rosa of the Instituto de Astrofisica de Canarias.
The study establishing IC 1101's physical edge was published in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.
If placed between the Milky Way and Andromeda, IC 1101 would almost bridge the entire distance between the two galaxies.
The main stellar body of IC 1101 extends to a radius of roughly 260 kiloparsecs (850,000 light-years) from its center.
A galaxy lacks a sharp, solid boundary and instead diffuses gradually into the surrounding cluster light.
IC 1101 is still actively growing and accumulating material in its outer regions.
Faint, plume-like outer structures around IC 1101 represent remnants of smaller galaxies destroyed by its gravitational field.
The Chandra X-ray Observatory has been used to conduct observations and surveys of the Abell 2029 cluster.

disputed: Earlier photographic plate measurements and different distance assumptions estimated IC 1101's outer diffuse halo at up to 6 million light-years (2 million light-years radius), but modern ultra-deep imaging defines the coherent main stellar body at 1.7 million light-years across. The script should specify that 1.7 million light-years is the robustly measured coherent stellar body, while diffuse halo material and past estimates reached larger scales.
